questions.prompt: What is the primary role of NavigationStack in SwiftUI?

options.text: It displays a root view and manages a stack of pushed child screens.
options.explanation: Right. NavigationStack presents a root view and manages screen transitions.

options.text: It replaces standard layout stacks like VStack and HStack on iPhone.
options.explanation: NavigationStack manages screen transitions, not basic view layout.

options.text: It stores network responses in persistent disk storage across launches.
options.explanation: NavigationStack handles screen hierarchies, not network caching.

options.text: It compiles Swift source code into machine binary code in the background.
options.explanation: Compiling Swift code is handled by the Swift compiler, not views.

questions.prompt: How do you associate a data value with a NavigationLink in modern SwiftUI?

options.text: By saving the data inside a UserDefaults key-value pair string.
options.explanation: Navigation links do not use UserDefaults for screen transitions.

options.text: By passing the value into the NavigationLink(value:) initializer.
options.explanation: Right. NavigationLink(value:) binds a data value to the link.

options.text: By adding a custom tag modifier with an integer index parameter.
options.explanation: The tag modifier is used in TabView or Picker, not NavigationLink values.

options.text: By encoding the data into an XML document and attaching a URL link.
options.explanation: SwiftUI uses native Swift types, not XML strings, for navigation.

questions.prompt: What modifier resolves a data value into a destination view in NavigationStack?

options.text: The .sheet(isPresented:) modal presentation view modifier.
options.explanation: The sheet modifier presents modal sheets, not pushed stack views.

options.text: The .onTapGesture modifier attached to the top navigation bar.
options.explanation: onTapGesture handles tap gestures, not type-based destination routing.

options.text: The .navigationDestination(for:destination:) view modifier.
options.explanation: Right. .navigationDestination maps value types to destination views.

options.text: The .overlay(alignment:) modifier placed on the master window scene.
options.explanation: Overlay layers views on top of each other without navigation stacks.

questions.prompt: What happens if you attach .navigationTitle directly to the NavigationStack container?

options.text: The navigation title renders in inverted colors across all child views.
options.explanation: SwiftUI does not invert colors when modifiers are misplaced.

options.text: The application immediately crashes with a fatal runtime exception.
options.explanation: Misplaced title modifiers compile and run without runtime crashes.

options.text: The navigation bar hides completely and removes the top back button.
options.explanation: Misplacing navigationTitle does not hide the navigation bar.

options.text: The navigation title does not appear because child views configure the bar.
options.explanation: Right. The active child view must configure the navigation bar title.

questions.prompt: Why is NavigationLink(destination: DetailView()) discouraged in long lists?

options.text: Because it creates destination views early for every row upfront.
options.explanation: Right. Early view creation wastes memory and slows down scrolling.

options.text: Because it disables user touch interactions across the entire device screen.
options.explanation: Touch interactions work normally with old NavigationLinks.

options.text: Because it limits the list container to displaying only ten total items.
options.explanation: NavigationLink has no item count restriction.

options.text: Because it prevents child views from applying standard foreground colors.
options.explanation: Colors function normally inside destination view bodies.

questions.prompt: Which protocol must custom data structs conform to when used as navigation values?

options.text: Comparable, so SwiftUI can sort screens in alphabetical order.
options.explanation: Comparable sorts items, but NavigationStack does not require sorting.

options.text: Hashable, so SwiftUI can uniquely identify and track destinations.
options.explanation: Right. NavigationStack requires values to conform to Hashable.

options.text: Codable, so SwiftUI can archive view hierarchies to disk drives.
options.explanation: Codable is used for saving path state, while Hashable is required for navigation values.

options.text: Identifiable, so SwiftUI can calculate dynamic row heights.
options.explanation: Identifiable is for collections; navigation values need Hashable.

questions.prompt: How can you programmatically push a new screen onto a NavigationPath?

options.text: By calling the presentModalViewController method on the key window.
options.explanation: presentModalViewController is a legacy UIKit method, not SwiftUI.

options.text: By posting an asynchronous notification to the default NotificationCenter.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter does not drive SwiftUI NavigationPath state.

options.text: By calling the append(_:) method on the bound NavigationPath instance.
options.explanation: Right. Appending a value to the path pushes the corresponding screen.

options.text: By modifying the root view controller frame dimensions in the AppDelegate.
options.explanation: Frame modifications do not trigger screen navigation pushes.

questions.prompt: Which modifier controls whether the navigation bar displays a large or compact title?

options.text: The .textScale modifier placed on the outer window root.
options.explanation: textScale affects text sizing, not navigation bar layout modes.

options.text: The .dynamicTypeSize modifier attached to the application delegate.
options.explanation: dynamicTypeSize sets font size ranges, not title display modes.

options.text: The .font(.headline) styling modifier attached to the list view.
options.explanation: font sets font attributes, not navigation bar display modes.

options.text: The .navigationBarTitleDisplayMode modifier placed on the child view.
options.explanation: Right. navigationBarTitleDisplayMode configures inline or large titles.

questions.prompt: What occurs when you nest a NavigationStack inside another NavigationStack?

options.text: It causes duplicate navigation bars and broken back navigation gestures.
options.explanation: Right. Nesting navigation stacks creates conflicting bars and gestures.

options.text: It automatically converts the layout into a split view on iPad devices.
options.explanation: Nesting stacks does not create NavigationSplitView layouts.

options.text: It compiles cleanly and optimizes screen transition animations automatically.
options.explanation: Nesting navigation stacks causes duplicate bars and broken back gestures.

options.text: It forces all child views to render in grayscale monochrome mode.
options.explanation: SwiftUI does not change color rendering when stacks are nested.

questions.prompt: What container should you use instead of NavigationStack for multi-column layouts on iPad?

options.text: UISplitViewControllerRepresentable wrapped in an individual view.
options.explanation: SwiftUI has native NavigationSplitView without UIKit wrappers.

options.text: NavigationSplitView, which supports sidebar, content, and detail columns.
options.explanation: Right. NavigationSplitView provides multi-column navigation on iPad.

options.text: TabView, which renders bottom bar tabs across the device display.
options.explanation: TabView creates tabbed pages, not multi-column sidebar split layouts.

options.text: LazyHStack, which lays out horizontal views inside a single screen.
options.explanation: LazyHStack lays out views in a row; it is not a navigation container.

questions.prompt: How does NavigationStack handle deep linking and state restoration?

options.text: By taking periodic screenshot bitmaps of the user display screen.
options.explanation: SwiftUI restores navigation state with data models, not screenshots.

options.text: By storing compiled C pointers in global kernel process registers.
options.explanation: SwiftUI does not manipulate raw kernel memory pointers.

options.text: By representing the entire navigation hierarchy as a collection of data.
options.explanation: NavigationStack stores routes as Hashable data values (and Codable values can be saved and restored).

options.text: By querying historical browser cache entries using WebKit protocols.
options.explanation: Native navigation does not interact with WebKit browser cache.

questions.prompt: What is the initial count of a newly created NavigationPath()?

options.text: 1, because the root view is counted as the initial path entry.
options.explanation: The root view is not stored in the path; the path holds pushed items.

options.text: Negative one, indicating that no navigation stack has been attached.
options.explanation: Path count is non-negative and represents stacked elements.

options.text: Undefined, because NavigationPath allocates memory lazily on demand.
options.explanation: NavigationPath count is an Int and equals 0 when initialized.

options.text: 0, because no destination items have been appended to the path yet.
options.explanation: Right. A freshly initialized NavigationPath is empty with count 0.

questions.prompt: How do you remove the top-most pushed screen from a NavigationPath?

options.text: By calling path.removeLast() on the bound NavigationPath instance.
options.explanation: Right. removeLast() pops the top screen from the navigation stack.

options.text: By invoking the popCurrentViewController global C function.
options.explanation: SwiftUI uses path mutations, not legacy C functions.

options.text: By setting the top screen alpha opacity property value to zero.
options.explanation: Hiding a view with opacity does not pop it from the navigation stack.

options.text: By disconnecting the mobile device from active internet connections.
options.explanation: Network status has no effect on navigation stack state.

questions.prompt: Why does NavigationStack improve list scrolling performance over NavigationView?

options.text: It caches pre-rendered bitmap images of all screens in device RAM.
options.explanation: NavigationStack does not pre-render offscreen bitmaps into RAM.

options.text: It waits to create destination views until a row is tapped.
options.explanation: Right. Lazy creation avoids building views for unvisited rows.

options.text: It uses Metal shaders to accelerate scrolling on older iPad devices.
options.explanation: NavigationStack manages screen hierarchies, not Metal shaders.

options.text: It prevents list items from executing custom tap gesture closures.
options.explanation: Tap gestures work normally inside NavigationStack list rows.

options.explanation: Right. It must be inside the stack so it can register destinations.

options.explanation: Navigation routing is declared in Swift code, not build settings.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import SwiftUI

var path = NavigationPath()
path.append("Detail")
print(path.count)

options.text: 1, because appending one string increases the path depth by one.
options.explanation: Right. Appending one item increases the path count from 0 to 1.

options.text: 0, because NavigationPath only stores Int identifiers.
options.explanation: NavigationPath accepts any Hashable value, including Strings.

options.text: 2, because NavigationPath automatically pushes a placeholder screen.
options.explanation: NavigationPath only contains elements explicitly appended.

options.text: It fails to compile because NavigationPath cannot be mutated with append.
options.explanation: NavigationPath provides a mutating append method.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import SwiftUI

var path = NavigationPath()
path.append("Screen1")
path.append("Screen2")
path.removeLast()
print(path.count)

options.text: 0, because removeLast removes all screens from the navigation path.
options.explanation: removeLast only removes one screen, not the entire path.

options.text: 1, because removeLast removes only the top screen from the path.
options.explanation: Right. Two items appended minus one item leaves one item.

options.text: 2, because removeLast fails silently when items are present.
options.explanation: removeLast mutates the path and removes the last item cleanly.

options.text: It fails to compile because removeLast does not exist on NavigationPath.
options.explanation: removeLast is a standard method on NavigationPath.

questions.prompt: Explain why Apple introduced NavigationStack in iOS 16 to replace NavigationView. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that NavigationView suffered from eager view creation and navigation glitches.
Explains that NavigationStack introduces data-driven navigation with NavigationLink(value:).
Mentions that destination views are created lazily only when tapped.

questions.modelAnswer: Apple replaced NavigationView because it created destination views early for every row, wasting memory. It also had navigation state bugs on iOS and iPadOS. In iOS 16, NavigationStack added a data-driven model using NavigationLink(value:). This pattern creates destination views lazily only when tapped and separates navigation state from views.

questions.prompt: Explain why placing .navigationTitle on the NavigationStack container fails to show a title. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that the navigation bar reflects the configuration of the currently active child view.
States that modifiers on NavigationStack apply to the container rather than the active screen.
Explains that the fix is to attach .navigationTitle to the child content view inside the stack.

questions.modelAnswer: In SwiftUI, the navigation bar displays titles based on the active child view currently shown on top of the stack. Attaching .navigationTitle to the NavigationStack container configures the outer wrapper instead of the displayed screen. Because the container has no active bar entry of its own, the title is ignored. To fix this issue, always attach .navigationTitle directly to the child view inside the stack.

questions.prompt: What is NavigationPath, and when should you use it instead of a typed array like [Route]? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that NavigationPath is a type-erased collection for mixed (heterogeneous) Hashable destinations.
Explains that a typed array like [Route] only holds a single (homogeneous) type.
Explains that NavigationPath should be used when a stack can push different data types.

questions.modelAnswer: NavigationPath is a type-erased collection that can store any Hashable data type. A Swift array like [Route] is homogeneous and only allows one data type on the stack. Use NavigationPath when your stack pushes mixed types, such as Strings, user profiles, and order details.

questions.prompt: How do you programmatically pop back to the root screen in a NavigationStack? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that navigation state is bound to a NavigationPath or array via NavigationStack(path: $path).
Explains that clearing the path triggers a pop to root.
States that SwiftUI automatically animates the transition back to the root screen.

questions.modelAnswer: To pop back to root programmatically, bind your NavigationStack to a NavigationPath state property using NavigationStack(path: $path). When you want to return to the root screen, reassign the path to a fresh NavigationPath() or call path.removeLast(path.count). SwiftUI detects the empty path and automatically animates the transition back to the root screen.

questions.prompt: Why must values passed to NavigationLink(value:) conform to Hashable? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that NavigationStack uses Hashable to track, compare, and match values to destinations.
Explains that SwiftUI matches the value type and identity against registered .navigationDestination blocks.
Mentions that missing Hashable conformance causes a compiler error.

questions.modelAnswer: Values passed to NavigationLink(value:) must conform to Hashable so SwiftUI can track and compare items across the stack. SwiftUI uses the value type and its hash value to match items to registered .navigationDestination(for:) closures. If a value does not conform to Hashable, the Swift compiler reports an error.
